claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5–1 wt.% well-dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles to CoCrFeNi will significantly reduce both friction coefficient and wear rate relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi.
The friction and wear reductions will be maintained from room temperature through 800 °C.
Y2O3 nanoparticles will enable in situ formation of a stable, lubricious oxide or glaze layer during sliding.
The Y2O3 content selected for the intervention is approximately 0.5–1 wt.%.
Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as nucleation sites for a continuous, adherent, and stable oxide or glaze tribolayer.
Reactive Y2O3 nanoparticles catalyze formation and stabilization of the lubricious oxide film.
The resulting oxide film lowers surface shear strength.
The tribofilm limits direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby reducing friction and slowing wear.
The Y2O3-triggered tribofilm will adapt its structure under changing thermal conditions and remain effective across the full temperature range.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi exhibits variable friction and accelerated wear because it forms protective surface films inconsistently during sliding.
The proposed intervention is effective under dry to mildly oxidative sliding conditions from ambient temperature to 800 °C.
The proposed intervention is effective at normal loads and sliding speeds typical of engineering applications.

A Ni50(AlNbTiV)50-based material achieved wear rates of approximately 10^-7 to 10^-6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C through adaptive interface protection, including a glaze layer at 800 °C.
In a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50-based coating system, Y2O3 additions reduced high-temperature friction and wear, with reported optima near 0.4–0.6 wt.% depending on the measured property.
Nano-Al2O3 addition to an Al-Cr-Fe-Ni-V alloy was associated with favorable hardness and wear resistance.
The dispersion quality, nanoparticle–matrix interface stability, and long-term tribolayer durability of Y2O3-modified CoCrFeNi remain unestablished.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in both friction coefficient and wear rate across all tested temperatures would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to reproducibly form a stable, continuous lubricious oxide tribolayer would falsify the proposed mechanism.
